comments.body:

To me this is similar to the way we trust the TLS stack not to leak its session keys. Eventually we trust the software/system, but we can increase the level of trust by using open source, formally validated software etc.

comments.author: ionut-arm
comments.body:
I think the attestation should always bind to either the (exported?) attestation secret, the TIK public key, or both. And the evidence MUST provide verifiable proof that links up to the code producing the attestation secret, or handling the TIK, that the software which generated the evidence is doing this stuff correctly. Otherwise you just can't trust the attestation credential.

To me this is more similar to the treatment of TIK - you need proof from the peer that the TIK is under their possession. If the TIK just signed ClientHello instead of the longer transcript required for CertificateVerify, that proof of possession is not enough.

issues.title: Application-level considerations
issues.author: burgerdev
issues.body:
The draft currently lists these advantages of intra-handshake:

https://github.com/yaronf/draft-fossati-seat-early-attestation/blob/4b45fe9cf52f1c58989daf9df0e3cea200ae0111/draft-fossati-seat-early-attestation.md?plain=1#L165-L169

Maybe it's a question of definitions, but I don't think this holds up in practice. There are several steps for producing and verifying evidence that don't sound like they can be solved with "At most, some configuration":

https://github.com/yaronf/draft-fossati-seat-early-attestation/blob/4b45fe9cf52f1c58989daf9df0e3cea200ae0111/draft-fossati-seat-early-attestation.md?plain=1#L374-L375

https://github.com/yaronf/draft-fossati-seat-early-attestation/blob/4b45fe9cf52f1c58989daf9df0e3cea200ae0111/draft-fossati-seat-early-attestation.md?plain=1#L330-L334

I guess these need to be implemented as callbacks to _some_ application code, since the TLS stack can't really know how to get or verify evidence by itself?

I would appreciate:

1. A section with API considerations (similar to https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9261#name-api-considerations).
2. A review of the above advantages based on those suggested APIs.

issues.title: Is the TIK protection requirement reasonable?
issues.author: burgerdev
issues.body:
The draft currently requires the TIK to be TEE-protected:

https://github.com/yaronf/draft-fossati-seat-early-attestation/blob/4b45fe9cf52f1c58989daf9df0e3cea200ae0111/draft-fossati-seat-early-attestation.md?plain=1#L182-L185

I understand the goal of the draft is to provide an attested TLS _session_. We already know from the post-handshake work that a trustworthy attested TLS session can be established with a long-term key that's not protected by a TEE. Why do we need it for intra-handshake?

The reason why this is important is that some flavours of TEEs are short-lived: confidential containers come to mind. It's probably infeasible to let all containers first do an ACME step (or similar) to get a certificate for their ephemeral key.

issues.title: Relationship of binder, evidence and CMW signing
issues.author: burgerdev
issues.body:
It's somewhat implict in the draft that the CMW needs to contain certain items and needs to be signed. For example, the draft says both:

https://github.com/yaronf/draft-fossati-seat-early-attestation/blob/4b45fe9cf52f1c58989daf9df0e3cea200ae0111/draft-fossati-seat-early-attestation.md?plain=1#L262-L265

https://github.com/yaronf/draft-fossati-seat-early-attestation/blob/4b45fe9cf52f1c58989daf9df0e3cea200ae0111/draft-fossati-seat-early-attestation.md?plain=1#L273-L276

To me, this implies that the binder is not included into the actual evidence, but somehow passed alongside it. (Otherwise, how could the AR be cached?)

It would be helpful if the draft was more specific about:

1. How to construct the binder.
2. How (whether) the binder needs to be tied to the evidence and laid out in the CMW.
3. What requirements apply to the CMW signature.

issues.title: Bring the I-D within SEAT charter
issues.author: yaronf
issues.body:
This is not a real issue, it's a suggested discussion framework so the editor team can reach consensus on an intra-handshake draft that maximizes our chances of falling inside the [SEAT charter](https://datatracker.ietf.org/group/seat/about/).

This issue depends heavily on Tiru's #35.

1. CMW transmitted as a new TLS message vs. TLS extension to Certificate message: it's clear that the latter is the only thing that'll keep us within charter. Downsides: the attested peer must have a certificate, so PSK is forever out of scope.
2. Binder:
2.1. Convince the WG that adding a new derivation step that does not affect the existing schedule is kosher.
2.2. Use only the ClientHello..ServerHello transcript.
2.3. Use the transcript as well as the TIK public key but do NOT derive from the handshake secrets. (Per paragraph (1) above, we're forced to use certificates anyway.)
3. Reattestation:
3.1. Do nothing: if you want reattestation, you should abort and restart the connection. This could work in the real world but some people want reattestation for long-lived connections.
3.2. EKU: we could use a subtype to extend EKU and add an EKU-Attestation message. The TLS WG might frown over this extension although formally it is legit.
3.3. CertUpdate: it's not clear to me that this is a viable option. Also, certificate updates are likely done less often that we might want for reattestation.

issues.title: Explicit TIK Public Key Claim vs. Implicit Nonce-Based Binding
issues.author: tireddy2
issues.body:
There are two possible approaches for binding the Evidence to the TLS connection and the key provenance of the TIK private key of TIK private key in the Evidence, and I’d like to discuss both and get feedback from the co-authors.

Option 1: Implicit binding via nonce construction

In this approach, the TLS stack constructs a nonce that embeds both the TLS handshake transcript hash and the hash of the TIK public key, and passes this nonce to the TEE. The TEE verifies that the embedded public key hash corresponds to a TIK private key it manages and, if so, signs the nonce as part of the Evidence.

On the Relying Party (RP) side, the RP reconstructs the expected nonce using the TLS handshake transcript hash and the hash of the TIK public key extracted from the end-entity certificate. The RP (or an external Verifier, if not co-located) verifies the TEE signature over the nonce. Successful verification allows the RP to infer that the TEE controls the TIK private key corresponding to the public key used in the TLS handshake, even though the key identity is not carried as an explicit claim in the Evidence.

This approach relies on correct nonce construction by the TLS stack and correct enforcement by the TEE, and the binding between the attestation and the key is inferred indirectly rather than expressed as an explicit Evidence claim.

Option 2: Explicit key identity claim in Evidence
In this approach, the Evidence itself carries an explicit claim, such as a hash of the public key (e.g., AIK_pub_hash). The nonce or challenge is used solely for freshness and channel binding. This allows the Relying Party to directly observe a statement like: “This Evidence attests to public key X,” rather than inferring the binding indirectly from how the nonce is constructed and validated by the TEE.

I prefer Option 2 as it would enable the Verifier to determine, based on attestation claims, whether the TIK private key is generated, stored, and protected within a secure element.

I think from a state machine POV it's easier to have Att before `EKU(new_key_update)`. It's also less confusing because you're still using the old traffic secrets to encrypt it (as we discussed, we cannot guarantee confidentiality against an active attacker anyway). Also, main_N+1 is already available at this point so I don't see why we couldn't have ATT *before* the EKU message. 

Lastly, including it before EKU(new_key_update) makes it simpler to include a hash of Att in EKU(new_key_update) itself - which is important for reliability, not for security. Think DTLS where the Att message gets dropped.

In our case, we need to send the Attestation message after EKU completes and after the “Use of Post-Handshake Authentication and Exported Authenticators with Extended Key Update” step in order to address the MITM attack described in https://github.com/tlswg/tls-key-update/pull/89, EKU by itself does not guarantee that both peers enter the same new key schedule; the authenticated transition is what detects any active interference.

Since attestation messages use the standard DTLS handshake re-transmission mechanism, reliability problem is already solved by the protocol. 

The sequencing I am proposing is:

1) Run EKU.
2) Perform the authenticated-transition step to ensure no MiTM.
3) Exchange attestation messages.

Happy to refine the wording further, but this seems like the cleanest and least invasive design.

An attacker that temporarily compromises an endpoint may later act as an active MitM capable of interfering with the EKU exchange. Such an attacker can cause the peers to transition to divergent traffic secrets without detection, but cannot compromise the endpoint to derive secrets after the new epoch is established. Yes, I will remove it.

>

> 2. Perform the authenticated-transition step to ensure no MiTM.
> 3. Exchange attestation messages.

And my proposal is:
1. Run first exchange of EKU.
2. Run second exchange of EKU, where the client and/or the server can prepend an Attestation message to the NKU.
3. Now that both are authenticated, transition the TLS state and accept attestation (e.g. dispatch a callback to the application).

> Happy to refine the wording further, but this seems like the cleanest and least invasive design.

Updated text as follows:

Reattestation is tied to the completion of an Extended Key Update (EKU) exchange {{!I-D.ietf-tls-extended-key-update}}. TLS peers that require reattestation MUST support EKU, Reattestation is always associated with the completion of an Extended Key Update (EKU) exchange since reattestation depends on the key schedule update defined in the EKU draft.
In TLS, Derive-Secret is typically used with the corresponding handshake messages as its input. Using the EKU messages follows that established pattern.

Yes, we need a call to discuss this. 
DTLS already defines an implicit acknowledgement mechanism for handshake messages, so Att does not need to define its own “ack”. DTLS ACK would suffice. 

NKU is designed for single purpose: acknowledgment of key schedule advancement. Allowing arbitrary handshake messages to precede it creates an interleaving of unrelated handshake flows, complicating the state machine.

Can you please explain the threat with my proposal ?

Thank you Tiru, I was not aware of the DTLS mechanism and the ACK message. My remaining concern is about the state machine: suppose I'm the server and I just completed EKU with the client, and I'm expecting an Attestation message from the client. How do I know when to expect it, and when am I allowed to fail the connection if I don't receive it?

The answer to this question is clear in my proposal, because as soon as NKU is received I know that the handshake is done. That's why I think this option simplifies rather than complicates the state machine.

I added a new section "DTLS considerations", please check. 

I now understand the problem with the state machine, I see two alternatives:

a) The `Attestation` message MUST be sent immediately before the attesting peer's `EKU(new_key_update)` message. However, the receiving peer MUST NOT process Attestation until the EKU exchange and the authenticated transition step have completed. This ensures that attestation bound to Main Secret N+1 is accepted only after both peers have confirmed that they share the same `Main Secret N+1`.

OR 

a) we could introduce a new TLS handshake message ("attestation_request") that can be sent after EKU and the authenticated-transition step are complete. The receiving peer would then send a regular Attestation handshake message, using the freshly derived attestation secret.

Option A is what I was proposing, and it still is my preference. (With one minor change, the protocol allows for *both* peers to attest).

comments.author: yaronf
comments.body:
@tireddy2 First of all, IIUC, this is not about a replay attack, it's about what I'll call "unauthorized provisioning of the TIK", i.e. an arbitrary server (not the TEE) being able to provision a certified TIK (CA-signed cert for an arbitrary private key) and then using it in our protocol.

I would claim that this attack is impossible if the endorsed software follows the protocol, specifically:

> The TEE itself, when possible, SHOULD generate the nonce by running HKDF with an allowlisted label and if it holds the TIK, SHOULD validate the pubic key.

Yes, this is a SHOULD and not a MUST, because we're trying to support multiple software architectures. And that may be something for us to discuss. But whenever the API into the TEE is wider than just a single nonce, this would mitigate this attack.

comments.body:

Just to be clear, the proposed text does not describe this as a replay attack. The intent is to capture exactly the scenario
you describe.

> 
> I would claim that this attack is impossible if the endorsed software follows the protocol, specifically:
> 
> > The TEE itself, when possible, SHOULD generate the nonce by running HKDF with an allowlisted label and if it holds the TIK, SHOULD validate the pubic key.
> 
> Yes, this is a SHOULD and not a MUST, because we're trying to support multiple software architectures. And that may be something for us to discuss. But whenever the API into the TEE is wider than just a single nonce, this would mitigate this attack.

I agree that in architectures where the TEE both generates the attestation secret and validates the TIK public key, the attack is mitigated. The difficulty is that the protocol cannot assume such an API across multiple architectures. From the relying party’s perspective, a compliant and a non-compliant implementation are indistinguishable unless the protocol requires the TEE to cryptographically bind the attestation secret to the TIK private key itself.

In split deployments, where TLS runs outside the TEE, attesting the TEE alone does not prove that the TIK private key used by TLS is the one generated and controlled by the TEE, so an explicit protocol-visible binding is still required.

In addition, an attacker can relay Evidence from a genuine TEE-based TLS endpoint to a non-TEE TLS stack, causing the relying party to accept a platform that is not actually executing the TLS endpoint. I think this is a mistake. Certificate updates happen on a much longer cadence, months or even years. Re-attestation might happen every few hours because it's much cheaper.

Moreover, the notion of an exported authenticator in the cert-update draft comes with all the baggage of post-handshake, i.e. the need for an extra messaging protocol (either on top of TLS or by reusing the TLS record protocol) that allows peers to distinguish between normal protected data and post-HS signaling. Alternatively, if EKU was defined to take extensions, we could include this extension in message 2+3 (to ensure a fresh binder derived from Main N+1).

Current practice increasingly relies on short-lived certificates (as discussed in the ACME WG), where certificate lifetimes may be on the order of days, making certificate refresh compatible with periodic re-attestation. 

CertificateUpdate is defined as a new TLS handshake message carrying an Exported Authenticator and is therefore a post-handshake signaling mechanism negotiated during the initial handshake. It is handled entirely by the TLS stack and does not require changes to the application.

Given what we say in L318-319:

> _"AttestationResults within the CMW MUST include a binder ensuring that the attestation is associated with this particular TLS connection”_

There should be no differences in freshness between BG check and Passport
Just to make sure, @thomas-fossati  - not my suggested change, right?

> > [..] An attacker cannot mount a successful attack
> 
> Tiru, which attack are you referring to here?

I am assuming an on-path adversary with full network visibility and the ability to modify, inject, or replay messages.

> 
> That said, the second sentence _“An attacker also […]”_ LGTM.
ok, so perhaps "An _active_ attacker” ?
I meant to say, a measured/signed TEE that has been verified (e.g. through manual code review) to implement this protocol correctly. I would appreciate a text proposal.

> Given what we say in L318-319:
> 
> > _"AttestationResults within the CMW MUST include a binder ensuring that the attestation is associated with this particular TLS connection”_
> 
> There should be no differences in freshness between BG check and Passport

But this is a discussion we need to have. It is quite possible that we will end up with multiple options.

New text: 

An active attacker cannot mount a successful attack because the attestation binder is derived from the TLS handshake transcript, including encrypted handshake messages that are not visible to eavesdroppers. An active attacker also cannot replay or relay attestation Evidence across TLS connections, since the attestation binder is bound to the specific TLS handshake transcript and the TLS identity key. Any attempt to reuse valid Evidence in a different TLS connection results in a binder mismatch and verification failure.
Looks good, but I don't like this kind of rationale in the normative text. Will include it in the "Security Properties" subsection a bit further down.

pulls.title: Add architecture diagram for TEE interface
pulls.author: yaronf
pulls.body:
## Summary

- Add architecture diagram showing TLS stack, Early Attestation Shim, and TEE layers
- Clarify the role of the shim between TLS and TEE
- Show data flows: transcript hash, TIK public key hash, nonce, and signed Evidence/AR
- Explain shim can be in TEE (better protection) or TLS stack (legacy TEE support)

Closes #41

comments.body:
nit: the labels are not centered.  One can sense that cursor has no eyes :-)

I can patch the three instances if you want.
Also add a number to the figure and refer it from the main body of the text
Sadly, it's not even Cursor. I've been using textik.com and my own eyes.

The following comments were discussed in today's call:

The evidence by the TEE has to capture the measurements of the TLS Stack and the Shim. If the TEE only reports its own state, the Verifier has no way of knowing if the Transcript Hash it received was generated by a legitimate TLS library or a malicious Shim.

The TEE interface will have to implement access control to verify the caller's identity. 
Without caller authentication, any process on the system could potentially send a dummy nonce to the TEE and receive a signed blob.

@tireddy2 What may need to be clarified further is that we get resistance to relay attacks only if the shim is part of the TEE. In other words, only if there are NO APIs into the TEE that bypass the shim.

I don't think access control (in the common understanding of the term) is even relevant here, because for access control you need an identity system and these are all internal components (e.g., the TLS stack) that don't have their own identity. The alternative to access control is very strict API design, such as "I sign an attestation for you only if it includes a public key and only I can associate that public key with a private key that I own".

@thomas-fossati had explained in the last week meeting that access control is possible. 

The other aspect is that even if the TLS Stack and the Shim are not located in the TEE, it is possible for the TEE to capture the measurements of the TLS Stack and the Shim.

I'd be happy to hear more from @thomas-fossati about access control.

Agree about measurements, and this is actually shown in the diagram that this PR adds - see the right-hand part about "measured and reported components".

> I'd be happy to hear more from @thomas-fossati about access control.
> 
> Agree about measurements, and this is actually shown in the diagram that this PR adds - see the right-hand part about "measured and reported components".

Yes, we discussed it would be helpful to add text as well about it.
